title: Revelation 17:7–18
context: The angel explains the beast that was, and is not, and is about to come, the seven heads as seven mountains and seven kings, and the ten horns as kings who will war against the Lamb. The Lamb will overcome them, and those with him are called, chosen, and faithful. In the end the beast and the horns turn on the prostitute and destroy her, because God put it into their hearts to fulfill his purpose.

verses.text: The angel said to me, “Why do you wonder? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has the seven heads and the ten horns.
verses.arminianNotes: The angel promises to explain the mystery.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God giving understanding.

verses.text: The beast that you saw was, and is not; and is about to come up out of the abyss and to go into destruction. Those who dwell on the earth and whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel when they see that the beast was, and is not, and shall be present.
verses.arminianNotes: Those whose names were not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will marvel at the beast. Arminian readers read the book of life in light of foreknowledge and continued faith, as in 3:5.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see here the clearest statement that names are written before creation, supporting unconditional election.
verses.keyContrast: This verse bears on election. Reformed readers see names written before creation, so the elect are kept from the beast’s deception. Arminian readers see God’s foreknowledge of those who would believe, with the book of life also linked to perseverance in 3:5.

verses.text: Here is the mind that has wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits.
verses.arminianNotes: The seven heads are seven mountains, often linked with Rome’s seven hills.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the widely accepted link with Rome.

verses.text: They are seven kings. Five have fallen, the one is, and the other has not yet come. When he comes, he must continue a little while.
verses.arminianNotes: Seven kings, five fallen, one is, one yet to come. Many attempt to match Roman emperors; others read seven as a symbolic number of completeness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers caution against precise schemes.

verses.text: The beast that was, and is not, is himself also an eighth, and is of the seven; and he goes to destruction.
verses.arminianNotes: The beast is an eighth and belongs to the seven.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see recurring opposition to God that goes to destruction.

verses.text: The ten horns that you saw are ten kings who have received no kingdom as yet, but they receive authority as kings with the beast for one hour.
verses.arminianNotes: Ten horns are ten kings who receive authority for one hour.

verses.text: These have one mind, and they give their power and authority to the beast.
verses.arminianNotes: They give their power to the beast.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see united opposition to God.

verses.text: These will war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will overcome them, for he is Lord of lords and King of kings; and those who are with him are called, chosen, and faithful.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Lamb will overcome them, and those with him are called, chosen, and faithful. Arminian readers stress that the chosen are also faithful, joining divine call and human faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the order of called, chosen, and faithful as reflecting God’s gracious choice that produces faithfulness.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm all three words. Reformed readers see election producing faithfulness. Arminian readers see calling, choosing, and faithful response held together without a sequence that makes faith the result of an unconditional decree.

verses.text: He said to me, “The waters which you saw, where the prostitute sits, are peoples, multitudes, nations, and languages.
verses.arminianNotes: The waters are peoples, multitudes, nations, and languages.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the world-wide reach of Babylon’s influence.

verses.text: The ten horns which you saw, they and the beast will hate the prostitute, will make her desolate, will strip her naked, will eat her flesh, and will burn her utterly with fire.
verses.arminianNotes: The beast and the horns turn on the prostitute and destroy her. Evil destroys itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see evil turning on evil under God’s judgment.

verses.text: For God has put in their hearts to do what he has in mind, to be of one mind, and to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God should be accomplished.
verses.arminianNotes: God put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose. Arminian readers see God working through the free choices of evil powers without causing their sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty over even the plans of his enemies, as in Proverbs 21:1.
verses.keyContrast: Both see God’s rule over history. Reformed readers see God directing even wicked hearts to fulfill his decree. Arminian readers see God using and permitting evil choices for his ends without being their author.

verses.text: The woman whom you saw is the great city which reigns over the kings of the earth.”
verses.arminianNotes: The woman is the great city that rules the kings of the earth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Rome in John’s day and the world city in every age.
